summary.text: Superfluidity is the property of a fluid with zero viscosity, so it flows without any loss of kinetic energy.
When stirred, a superfluid forms vortices that continue to rotate indefinitely.
It occurs in the two helium isotopes, helium-3 and helium-4, when liquefied by cooling to cryogenic temperatures, and is theorized in other exotic states of matter.

facts.label: Discovered
facts.value: In helium-4 by Kapitsa, and independently by Allen and Misener, in 1937

facts.label: Accepted theory
facts.value: Lev Landau's macroscopic theory for helium-4, from 1941

facts.label: Helium-3 prize
facts.value: Its superfluidity earned the 1996 Nobel Prize in Physics

facts.label: Neutron stars
facts.value: Arkady Migdal first proposed superfluidity inside them

items.prompt: A superfluid is stirred. What happens to the vortices it forms?

options.label: They die out as friction turns motion into heat
They keep rotating indefinitely
They split into smaller ones that stop at once
They rotate faster until the fluid boils

items.explain: A superfluid has zero viscosity and flows without any loss of kinetic energy, so stirred vortices continue to rotate indefinitely.

items.prompt: A student claims every Bose–Einstein condensate is a superfluid. What is the correction?

options.label: The two often occur together but are not directly related
They are the same thing under two names
Every superfluid is a condensate, but not the reverse
Only condensates made from helium count as superfluids

items.explain: Superfluidity often co-occurs with condensation, but neither is directly related to the other, so not all condensates are superfluids and not all superfluids are condensates.

items.prompt: Why does helium-4 become superfluid at far higher temperatures than helium-3?

options.label: Helium-3 atoms are heavier, so they stay warm longer
Helium-4 atoms are fermions that pair up easily
Helium-3 atoms cannot be liquefied by cooling at all
Helium-4 atoms are bosons, but helium-3 atoms must pair first

items.explain: Each helium-4 atom is a boson, but a helium-3 atom is a fermion that can form bosons only by pairing, which occurs at much lower temperatures.

items.prompt: Superfluid vacuum theory treats the physical vacuum as what, and what is its goal?

options.label: A solid, aiming to explain helium-3
A gas of fermions, aiming to cool atoms
A superfluid, aiming to unify quantum mechanics with gravity
A condensate, aiming to measure viscosity

items.explain: Superfluid vacuum theory views the physical vacuum as a superfluid, with the goal of unifying quantum mechanics with gravity.

items.prompt: Why have some compared starling murmurations to superfluidity?

options.label: Starlings fly through the air without any friction at all
Their rapid flight-pattern changes mimic the phase change toward superfluidity
Starlings cool the surrounding air to cryogenic temperatures
Starling flocks form real vortices of liquid helium overhead

items.explain: The rapidity of change in flight patterns mimics the phase change leading to superfluidity in some liquid states.

items.prompt: Helium-3 atoms pair up before they become superfluid. What is that process similar to?

options.label: Electron pairing in superconductivity
Starlings pairing off in flight
Light quanta combining into photons
Salt ions pairing in water

items.explain: A helium-3 atom forms bosons by pairing with another like itself, a process similar to the electron pairing in superconductivity.
